title: Betting on Autonomous Aircraft
gist: In a Cogs of War interview, Shield AI co-founder Brandon Tseng argues that world-class autonomy software combined with purpose-built hardware, not the airframe alone, is the durable defense advantage, and that autonomy and military intelligence are chronically underfunded relative to weapons. He details Shield AI's Hivemind, V-BAT, and the runway-independent X-BAT, and warns that much of what the U.S. and Taiwan are buying will fail once China jams GPS and communications.

insights.claim: Shield AI co-founder Brandon Tseng now expects autonomous systems for defense to become ubiquitous by 2040-2045, revising his original 2015 estimate of 2035 because he underestimated how long Pentagon procurement and investor appetite would take to catch up.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: A pushed-out adoption timeline tempers near-term defense-autonomy revenue expectations even as the secular thesis holds.
insights.quote: Now I actually think autonomous systems for defense will become ubiquitous by 2040–2045, versus my original 2035 estimate.
insights.locator: In 2015, I believed the fringe position

insights.claim: When Shield AI raised money in 2015 it met 30 Silicon Valley investors who all said no, and the next year met 25 more of whom only two said yes, with a16z's Peter Levine likening defense tech to contrarian bets like Uber or Airbnb.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Frames defense tech's shift from uninvestable to consensus, useful context for judging whether current valuations have overshot.
insights.quote: ideas that look dumb until they don’t
insights.locator: In August 2015, we met with 30 investors

insights.claim: Tseng disputes that Shield AI treats the aircraft as unimportant, arguing the durable competitive advantage comes from combining world-class autonomy software with world-class hardware built for specific missions.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Positions Shield AI as an integrated software-plus-hardware play rather than a pure-software vendor, affecting how to value it against peers.
insights.quote: We believe the combination of world-class software and world-class aircraft and hardware will lead to a durable competitive advantage
insights.locator: I disagree with the premise

insights.claim: Shield AI targets only large markets where it can achieve at least a 10x improvement in price-performance, citing V-BAT doing Predator's missions at 10x better overall cost and X-BAT aiming to do fighter and bomber missions at a fraction of total cost.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: A 10x price-performance bar is a concrete screen for which unmanned programs can displace legacy platforms.
insights.quote: We’re looking for a large market opportunity where we can achieve a minimum 10 times improvement in price-performance.
insights.locator: The saying “hardware is hard”

insights.claim: Shield AI's Hivemind AI pilot has flown on more than 30 platforms across air, sea, and land, including V-BAT, Anduril's YFQ-44A, Airbus helicopters, and Ukrainian one-way attack drones, deliberately avoiding lock-in to a single hardware manufacturer.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Hardware-agnostic autonomy is a moat and a lock-in play across the unmanned ecosystem, including rivals' airframes.
insights.quote: Our AI Pilot Hivemind has flown on more than 30 platforms across air, sea, and land
insights.locator: We’re very deliberate about what we choose to build

insights.claim: Shield AI's integration time has collapsed as its architecture matured: three years to fly an AI pilot on the F-16, 120 days on a Kratos Firejet, and now under two weeks for two engineers to build and fly an AI pilot on a one-way attack drone, with about 90% of the software carrying over between platforms.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Compounding software reuse is the scalability evidence that separates a durable autonomy platform from a bespoke integrator.
insights.quote: It took Shield AI three years to get an AI pilot flying on the F-16. The same work on a Kratos Firejet took 120 days.
insights.locator: The biggest lesson from being involved in that many platforms

insights.claim: Tseng argues military intelligence is dangerously underattended because weapons only work if you know where to point them, noting the U.S. struggled to find mobile Iraqi Scud launchers in the Gulf War and has lost roughly 50 Predator drones since 2023 to cheap, mobile weapon systems.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Points investment toward persistent tactical ISR rather than munitions, where Tseng sees the real capability gap.
insights.quote: weapons only work if you know where to point them
insights.locator: Everyone wants to talk about missiles and munitions

insights.claim: Tseng estimates that over a 24-hour period current forces cover less than 10% of the significant terrain in a warzone, because there is no infrastructure connecting strategic surveillance to tactical drones that can loiter over contested terrain and feed units real-time intelligence.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Identifies a 'missing middle layer' of persistent tactical ISR as the addressable gap Shield AI's V-BAT is aimed at.
insights.quote: we probably cover less than 10 percent of the significant terrain in a given warzone
insights.locator: Right now, across a 24-hour period

insights.claim: Tseng told Congress that autonomy is now more important than stealth or GPS satellites were when introduced, but its budget is not taken seriously because it is software, which the Pentagon still expects to be nearly free.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: A cultural underpricing of software creates upside if defense budgets re-rate autonomy toward hardware-like line items.
insights.quote: The Pentagon still treats software as something that should be nearly free.
insights.locator: Part of that is a cultural problem

insights.claim: Tseng points to the Collaborative Combat Aircraft and Low-Cost Unmanned Combat Attack System programs as the first real attempts to fund autonomy and mass together rather than as separate problems.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Names the specific programs of record where autonomy funding is actually flowing, useful for tracking demand.
insights.quote: the first real attempt to fund autonomy and mass together, instead of treating them as separate problems
insights.locator: That’s starting to change

insights.claim: Tseng argues satellites are being wrongly treated as a replacement for the middle layer of drones rather than a complement, because satellites can tell you something moved in a region but cannot loiter for hours to tell a commander exactly what it was and whether it is a threat, even without communications or GPS.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the capital rush into space-based sensing and argues air-breathing autonomy retains a distinct role.
insights.quote: orbit is often treated as a replacement for that middle layer of drones rather than a complement
insights.locator: A lot of money and attention is flowing toward space-based sensing

insights.claim: Because satellites can be jammed or degraded and are themselves targets, Tseng argues forces need ISR that does not depend on a signal from space and must ration whatever satellite bandwidth survives a fight.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Contested-space assumptions favor resilient, connectivity-independent airborne ISR over pure space architectures.
insights.quote: Satellites are also a target.
insights.locator: Satellites are also a target

insights.claim: The war in Ukraine forced Shield AI to make zero dependency on connectivity a hard design requirement, because Russia sustains more than 200 Shahed-class drone launches a day while GPS is constantly jammed and communications spoofed.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Connectivity-independence is becoming a baseline spec, disqualifying systems that rely on live links or GPS.
insights.quote: Ukraine forced us to design for zero dependency on connectivity as a hard requirement.
insights.locator: Ukraine forced us to design for zero dependency

insights.claim: Tseng was surprised and angered that many U.S. companies left Ukraine once easy American government money stopped flowing, arguing this abandonment leaves U.S. equipment untested and likely to fail on a real battlefield.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: A battlefield track record in Ukraine becomes a differentiator; firms that stayed may hold a real edge.
insights.quote: how so many U.S. companies left Ukraine after the American government’s easy money stopped flowing
insights.locator: What has surprised me

insights.claim: Ukraine's domestically built tactical drones are effective only from zero to roughly 30 kilometers, and Tseng sees rising demand for deep-strike systems that hit targets which change a campaign's trajectory.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: The range gap points to a growing deep-strike market segment that Shield AI says it is building toward.
insights.quote: Their domestically built systems are effective from zero to roughly 30 kilometers
insights.locator: how far Ukraine’s own tactical drone ecosystem has gone

insights.claim: Shield AI's X-BAT runs on a GE F110 engine producing around 29,000 pounds of thrust, versus the roughly 3,000-pound business-jet-class engines on most Collaborative Combat Aircraft, giving it about three times the payload, two to three times the electrical power, and the ability to operate without a crewed aircraft nearby on a fighter or bomber mission in the Pacific.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: X-BAT is positioned as a fighter/bomber-class autonomous aircraft, a different and larger market than wingman drones.
insights.quote: X-BAT runs on a GE F110, the same class of engine that powers the F-16, generating around 29,000 pounds of thrust.
insights.locator: This is a deliberate bet

insights.claim: Tseng argues runway-dependent airpower is a liability against a peer adversary because runways, carrier decks, and fuel infrastructure are targeted to neutralize airpower before launch, and cites the United States losing billions of dollars in aircraft parked on runways in the opening days of the conflict with Iran.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Elevates runway-independence and dispersal as a survivability requirement, favoring systems like X-BAT that relaunch from ships, islands, or bare ground.
insights.quote: Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East made clear that runway-dependent airpower is a liability against a peer adversary.
insights.locator: It was not designed against a Collaborative Combat Aircraft requirement

insights.claim: X-BAT is designed to carry the same internal weapons payload as an F-35 with greater range, and to relaunch from a ship, island, or bare patch of ground and move every 15 to 30 minutes so there is no fixed target to hit, which Tseng notes matters for Taiwan's few, easily located runways.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Mobility-based survivability is the design pitch aimed directly at a Taiwan-contingency airbase-vulnerability problem.
insights.quote: it can move every 15 to 30 minutes, so there’s no fixed target to hit
insights.locator: Taiwan has a similar problem

insights.claim: Tseng warns that across defense tech, valuations have run ahead of revenue growth and capture of programs of record, and says a company earns higher valuations only by repeatedly delivering battlefield outcomes at increasing scale.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: A sector insider flagging a valuation-versus-delivery gap is a caution signal for defense-tech investors.
insights.quote: Valuations shouldn’t run too far ahead of your revenue growth or capture of programs of record.
insights.locator: Defense tech has attracted enormous capital

insights.claim: Tseng argues too many systems being sold to Taiwan, including GPS-dependent precision weapons and any system needing a live human video or control link, will become useless once China turns off GPS and communications, and urges testing every weapon in a jammed environment or requiring a Ukraine track record.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: A jamming-survivability test becomes the key procurement filter for Taiwan and U.S. buyers, reshaping which vendors win.
insights.quote: too many things are being purchased or recommended to Taiwan that will simply fail when China turns off GPS and communications
insights.locator: Where do you think the conventional wisdom

insights.claim: Tseng says the United States cannot match China's production alone because China has two to three times the industrial capacity, installed nearly ten times as many industrial robots in 2024, and spends roughly ten times more on industrial subsidies relative to its economy, but that the U.S. plus allies including Taiwan, Japan, Australia, South Korea, the Philippines, and India together likely exceed China's capacity.
insights.speaker: Brandon Tseng
insights.so_what: Reframes the industrial-base competition as coalition-versus-China, favoring allied co-production and partnership plays.
insights.quote: China has two to three times the industrial capacity of the United States, installed nearly ten times as many industrial robots in 2024
insights.locator: The conventional wisdom I’d push back on
